rv.q: And Stephens's claim that the play is charged with the spirit of Patti Smith's Birdland, about a boy's longed-for reunion with his father, is confirmed by Paul's own awkward backstage encounter with the dad he has long since discarded. Scott's performance catches perfectly Paul's weird contradictions.

Paul is at once mythic (for the world of the play is one in which record companies underwrite acts to an extent unseen for decades in the real world) and, through the cracks in the icon, still vestigially human.
Andrew Scott's extraordinary performance lights up Simon Stephens’s new play about a rock god losing his mind.
In Mike Bartlett's fine new play at the Almeida, the Windsors acquire Shakespearean depths, while the ravages of a rock-star life dazzle at the Royal Court

For all the air of experiment in the abstract staging and multiple role-play of Carrie Cracknell's striking production, Stephens's drama, which is named after the Patti Smith song, is only intermittently successful at bursting through the cliches of the rock-rake's-progress.

The result, greatly helped by Ian MacNeil’s design, is a series of vivid images that compensate for an absence of substance. At times, the text is rather banal and repetitive, and the few good ideas are rather thinly spread.
I left the theatre with a taste of disappointment on my tongue.

cn.t: Andrew Scott's magnetic performance as a self-destructing rock star earns near-universal praise, but critics are split on Stephens' script—some find it a compelling character study, others too tame to fully unnerve.
